title: Godzilla Just Picked a Fight With Ramayana. Diwali 2026 Has Become the Biggest Box Office War in Indian History.
excerpt: The Oscar-winning monster franchise dropped a teaser timed to Diwali — the same weekend India's ₹4,000-crore mythological epic needs every IMAX screen on the planet.
body:
The monster has picked his date. And he has chosen the worst possible enemy.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=Xmy-Z3dHMd8</youtube>

**Godzilla Minus Zero** — the sequel to the Oscar-winning *Godzilla Minus One* — dropped its first teaser this week, confirming a worldwide IMAX release timed directly to Diwali 2026. Which means it lands on the same weekend as **Ramayana: Part One**, the most expensive Indian film ever made, starring **Ranbir Kapoor**, **Sai Pallavi**, and **Yash**, with a combined two-part budget north of ₹4,000 crore.

This isn't a scheduling accident. It's a war for IMAX screens — and the diaspora is the battlefield.

## What the Teaser Reveals

Director **Takashi Yamazaki** is not making a trilogy. "There won't be a third time. It ends here," he said in a translated statement that immediately set the internet ablaze.

The teaser picks up in 1949, two years after the events of *Minus One*, with the Shikishima family facing a new calamity. **Ryunosuke Kamiki** and **Minami Hamabe** return as Koichi and Noriko, and humanity has apparently resorted to a nuclear bomb in a last-ditch effort to halt Godzilla's rampage.

The first film was a phenomenon. Made for a reported $15 million — a fraction of Hollywood's blockbuster budgets — it became the first non-English-language film to win the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects, beating *Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3*, *The Creator*, and *Mission: Impossible – Dead Reckoning*. It grossed over $100 million worldwide. A sequel with a bigger budget and a final-chapter narrative? The anticipation is enormous.

## Why Ramayana Can't Afford to Share

Here's the math that keeps **Namit Malhotra** and Prime Focus Studios up at night: India has fewer than 30 IMAX screens. Thirty. For a film that needs to recover ₹4,000 crore across two parts, the domestic premium market is a boutique showcase, not a recovery engine.

**Ramayana: Part One** was supposed to own Diwali. The trailer drops July 24 at a grand worldwide premiere. The film arrives in IMAX during the Diwali window (reportedly November 8). Directed by **Nitesh Tiwari** (the man behind *Dangal*), scored by **A.R. Rahman** and **Hans Zimmer** together, starring Ranbir as Lord Ram, Sai Pallavi as Sita, Yash as Ravana, and **Sunny Deol** as Hanuman — it's designed to be India's answer to the global cinematic epic.

But "India's answer" requires global screens. For Ramayana to breathe financially, it needs the 1,700-plus IMAX screens across North America, Europe, and the Middle East — the same screens Godzilla Minus Zero will be fighting for. And unlike a typical Bollywood release that plays to its own audience, Ramayana's visual-effects ambitions demand the premium large-format experience. Standard screens won't do the work justice or the numbers.

## The Full Diwali–Christmas Landscape

The collision extends well beyond these two. Here's what the second half of 2026 looks like at the Indian box office:

**August 14 (Independence Day):** **Awarapan 2** (Emraan Hashmi's cult sequel) vs **Batwara 1947** (Sunny Deol reunites with Rajkumar Santoshi in a Partition drama featuring **Aamir Khan** and **A.R. Rahman**)

**September 25:** **The Vvaan** (**Sidharth Malhotra** and **Tamannaah Bhatia**) stakes out an early autumn slot

**October–November (Diwali window):** **Ramayana: Part One** vs **Godzilla Minus Zero** — the headliner clash. Both need IMAX. Only one can have the screens on day one.

**December 18 (Christmas corridor):** **Avengers: Doomsday** (Robert Downey Jr. returns to the MCU as Doctor Doom) vs **Dune: Part Three** — two Hollywood titans sharing a release date. And somewhere nearby, **Shah Rukh Khan's King** (with daughter **Suhana Khan** making her theatrical debut, directed by Siddharth Anand) is targeting the Christmas window.

The second half of 2026 is the most loaded release calendar in Indian box-office history. Every holiday weekend has at least two behemoths scheduled.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs in New York, London, Toronto, and Dubai, the Diwali weekend has always been sacred cinema time — the one window where Indian films get premium screen allocation at Western multiplexes. Ramayana was counting on that loyalty.

But Godzilla Minus Zero isn't some obscure art-house release. The first film was a crossover hit with Western audiences. It won an Oscar. It played in IMAX globally. The sequel will command significant screen real estate in exactly the markets Ramayana needs.

The result is a genuine fight for the diaspora's attention — and wallet. Do you go see India's biggest-ever mythological epic in IMAX on Diwali weekend, or do you choose the final chapter of an Oscar-winning Japanese franchise? If you're in a city with only two or three IMAX screens, you might not get both.

India's theatrical ambitions have never been higher. But neither has the competition. The stages are getting bigger, the budgets are getting more obscene, and the calendar has never been more ruthless. Welcome to Bollywood's most expensive game of chicken.
